own_scenes.desc: En 1966 la homosexualidad era ilegal en Reino Unido y en Estados Unidos; Time la llamaba «enfermedad perniciosa» y el 82 % de los varones americanos la creía dañina. La generación de Joe Meek y Brian Epstein (ambos detenidos por «importunar» y chantajeados) había interiorizado ese odio. En Reino Unido, tras el informe Wolfenden (1957) y la campaña de la Homosexual Law Reform Society, Lord Arran sacó adelante en los Lores un proyecto en junio de 1966 y Leo Abse presentó el suyo en julio. En Estados Unidos había mucho activismo de base y poco efecto legal: la Mattachine Society (1951), ONE, The Ladder, el congreso ECHO de 1965 («The Homosexual in the Great Society»), el «sip-in» de abril de 1966 y, junto a ellos, las revistas de físico y los discos de Camp Records. En julio de 1966 nació en el Tenderloin de San Francisco Vanguard, organización de chaperos, «hair fairies» y jóvenes sin hogar; en agosto estalló el primer motín gay en la cafetería Compton’s. En Londres el camp de Joe Orton y de Julian y Sandy (Round the Horne) llegaba al gran público, los mods y los gais compartían tiendas de Carnaby Street (Vince, John Stephen) y anfetaminas, y Le Duce abrió como un Scene gay con Motown y ska.

refs.q: In both the US and the UK, the physical expression of homosexuality was totally illegal.
refs.para: There was no thought that these records would sell outside the ghetto. In both the US and the UK, the physical expression of homosexuality was totally illegal. The author and researcher Patrick Higgins points to at least eight specific charges that could be brought against practising homosexuals in the UK. The situation was similar in the US, although the exact restrictions varied from state to state. Quite apart from legal sanctions, public opinion was hostile.
refs.chapter: Agosto: Do You Come Here Often? Joe Meek, los derechos gais y un verano de violencia

refs.q: By 1966, there was a fresh urgency on the part of homophile groups in both the US and the UK.
refs.para: By 1966, there was a fresh urgency on the part of homophile groups in both the US and the UK. Although these organisations were entirely separate from the world of clothes, drugs, music, clubs and sex – speeding mods tended not to care about the law, until it laid its gnarled hand on their shoulder – they had been touched by the same sense that things had to change and that the time, if it was not right now, had to come soon.
refs.chapter: Agosto: Do You Come Here Often? Joe Meek, los derechos gais y un verano de violencia

refs.q: In the same month that this issue of Vanguard was published, there was the first gay riot
refs.para: In the same month that this issue of Vanguard was published, there was the first gay riot, when about fifty or sixty young queers and drag queens erupted in fury inside an establishment, Gene Compton’s Cafeteria, that they felt to be a safe haven. Infuriated by heavy-handed and intrusive policing, a young transvestite threw coffee over an aggressive cop, and the other customers went on the rampage.
refs.chapter: Agosto: Do You Come Here Often? Joe Meek, los derechos gais y un verano de violencia

refs.q: WE HAVE HEARD TOO MUCH ABOUT “WHITE POWER” AND “BLACK POWER” SO GET READY TO HEAR ABOUT “STREET POWER”.
refs.para: As if to clear the air, Vanguard organised a ‘clean sweep’ by hair fairies in Market Street shortly afterwards, with a press release that stated their position: ‘the VANGUARD demonstration indicates the willingness of society’s outcasts to work openly for an improvement in their own social-economic power. WE HAVE HEARD TOO MUCH ABOUT “WHITE POWER” AND “BLACK POWER” SO GET READY TO HEAR ABOUT “STREET POWER”.’
refs.chapter: Agosto: Do You Come Here Often? Joe Meek, los derechos gais y un verano de violencia
